Select rows by position

Source: R/slice.R
slice.tbl_gpu.Rd

Keeps rows of a GPU table by integer position, as dplyr::slice() does. Constant positions run on the GPU, ungrouped, after group_by() and with .by. With groups, only a strictly increasing positive index vector or a set of negative indices runs on the GPU (an ungrouped table also takes duplicated and reordered positions; see ... below). Anything else runs in dplyr on the CPU (see cuplyr-fallback): an index expression that needs the data, e.g. one that reads a column or n(), or a grouped or .by index vector with duplicated or reordered positions.

Usage

# S3 method for class 'tbl_gpu'
slice(.data, ..., .by = NULL, .preserve = FALSE)

Arguments

.data

A tbl_gpu object created by tbl_gpu().

...

Integer row positions, e.g. slice(df, 1:3). Duplicates and reordering are allowed for positive indices when .data is ungrouped and .by= isn't supplied (slice(df, c(3, 1, 1))); grouped or .by calls run on the GPU only for a strictly increasing, duplicate-free positive index vector (and on the CPU otherwise); negative indices drop those rows instead (order/duplicates never matter here, grouped or not); 0/NA are silently dropped; out-of-range positions are silently dropped; positive and negative indices cannot be mixed.

.by

Optional grouping columns for this call only, run on the GPU. As in dplyr, the result has the groups in the order each one first appears in .data, and it is ungrouped. Supplying .by when .data is already grouped (via group_by()) is an error, as in dplyr.

.preserve

Whether to keep the groups the slice emptied. With TRUE, a group_by()-grouped result keeps the input's group keys (empty groups included) for group_data(), collect() and summarise(), like dplyr (see group_by.tbl_gpu() for what carries them on). On a .drop = FALSE table every group is kept whatever .preserve says, as in dplyr (also for slice_head(), slice_tail(), slice_min() and slice_max()).

Value

A tbl_gpu object with the selected rows.

Details

Row order

As in dplyr: ungrouped, the rows come in the order of the positions. After group_by() the result comes group by group, in ascending group-key order (an NA key last), and each group's rows keep their order. With .by the groups come in the order each first appears in .data.
